### Lighthouse

After the sea went away, we kept the lighthouse.

It stood above a desert of rippled sand, its red paint peeling, its stairs worn smooth by three generations of our family. Far below, fishing boats lay where they had settled: hulls split open, nets reduced to grey thread, gulls nesting in the rusted engines.

There was no water left to warn ships about.

Still, every evening, my grandmother climbed the two hundred and twelve steps and lit the lamp.

“Waste of oil,” the village said.

“A light isn’t oil,” she answered. “A light is a decision.”

When she became too weak to climb, I carried the fuel for her. When her hands began to shake, I trimmed the wick. When she could no longer leave her bed, she listened for the mechanism’s slow rotation and knew, by some private arithmetic, whether I had done it properly.

One winter night, I asked her who she thought was still out there.

She looked toward the black window.

“Someone,” she said.

After she died, the village stopped delivering oil. I used my own savings. Then I burned furniture, fence posts, the doors of abandoned houses. People thought grief had made me stupid. Perhaps it had.

On the last night, with nothing left to burn, I climbed to the lamp room and watched the flame shrink.

Below me lay the dry Atlantic. Above me, cold stars.

The flame went out.

For the first time in a hundred and forty years, the lighthouse was dark.

Then, far overhead, one star moved.

It stopped.

Moved again.

Three times: a long passage, a short one, a long one.

My grandmother’s signal.

I laughed so hard I had to sit down on the iron floor.

All those years, she had not been keeping the light for ships. She had been answering.

Somewhere beyond the dry Atlantic, beyond the moon, something enormous adjusted its course.
